title: Collections and recursion
sub: Remove inside foreach, an endless tree walk and height comparison
cards/0/body: You read a list aloud, page after page. Suddenly someone tears out a page while you are reading. You lose your place and do not know what to read next. A foreach over a List behaves the same way and gives up loudly: it throws InvalidOperationException, "Collection was modified".
cards/0/deep: List<T> has a version counter. Every Add/Remove bumps it, and at the start of each step the enumerator compares its own copy of the version with the current one. A mismatch means an exception. For Dictionary in .NET Core 3.0+, Remove and Clear during enumeration do not bump the version and are therefore allowed. But in .NET Framework and in Unity (the Mono class library, under both Mono and IL2CPP) the dictionary works the old way, and such a loop throws too. Code that "worked" in tests on .NET 8 will crash in Unity.
cards/1/q: What happens when RemoveResolved runs and the list contains a resolved clash?
cards/1/options/0: InvalidOperationException on the next step of the loop
cards/1/options/1: The resolved clashes are quietly removed
cards/1/explain: After Remove, the list version has changed, and the next step of the enumeration notices. Besides, every Remove searches for the item and shifts the tail: that is O(n) per removal.
cards/1/wrong/1: It would be quiet if you removed outside the loop or used RemoveAll.
cards/1/wrong/2: The list is not cleared entirely: the loop is simply cut short by an exception.
cards/2/q: Replace the loop with a single call: remove all resolved items in one pass.
cards/2/explain: RemoveAll walks the list once, shifts the survivors itself and takes the condition directly. That is O(n) instead of O(n²). Do not forget to reset the cache afterwards, because it still holds stale queries.
cards/3/q: Which ways safely remove items from List<Clash>? Pick all that apply.
cards/3/options/1: for (int i = _clashes.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--) with RemoveAt(i)
cards/3/explain: RemoveAll is the fastest. A loop from the end does not shift indexes you have not visited yet. A copy via ToList is safe, but costs more time and memory. A direct foreach with Remove crashes.
cards/4/body:
CollectFloor calls itself for every child. Each call puts a new plate on a "stack of plates" (the call stack). If the data contains a ring (an element is its own descendant), the plates never run out until the stack collapses.

This crash is called StackOverflowException, and it has a harsh trait: in .NET you cannot catch it with try/catch. The whole process terminates.
cards/4/deep: A thread's stack is limited (around 1 MB in a typical setup; other platforms and thread pool threads can differ). A depth of tens of thousands of frames can kill the process even without any ring: a very deep tree from an imported model is enough. The C# compiler does not do tail-call optimization, and you cannot rely on the JIT for it either. A Unity caveat: Mono in the Editor sometimes turns the overflow into a regular exception in the console, and the Editor survives. That is no protection: in an IL2CPP build on a device the same error usually means an app crash.
cards/5/q: Can you wrap the CollectFloor call in try/catch (Exception) and carry on calmly?
cards/5/options/0: No: in .NET StackOverflowException cannot be caught, the process dies
cards/5/explain: Since .NET 2.0, the CLR terminates the process immediately on a stack overflow: carrying on with an exhausted stack is not safe. You have to defend in advance: limit the depth or walk the tree without recursion.
cards/5/wrong/1: For a stack overflow, no catch block is ever invoked.
cards/5/wrong/2: That exception type exists, but in .NET no catch clause ever receives it.
cards/6/task: Three service methods. Each hides its own bug about collections, traversal or numbers. Find all three.
cards/6/bugs/0/why: The list changes during enumeration, and the next step throws InvalidOperationException. Also, each removal shifts the tail, so the work is quadratic.
cards/6/bugs/1/title: Recursion with no guard against cycles or depth
cards/6/bugs/1/why: If Parent and Children form a ring (or the tree is just very deep), the stack overflows. In .NET StackOverflowException cannot be caught: the whole app goes down instead of reporting an error.
cards/6/bugs/2/why: After calculations a height can differ in the last digit. An element that stands on the level is not recognized as such, and the floor looks "empty".
cards/7/q: Put the steps of an iterative walk (no recursion, protected from rings) in order.
cards/7/items/0: Push the root onto a Stack and create a HashSet of visited nodes
cards/7/items/1: While the stack is not empty, pop the top node
cards/7/items/2: If the node was already visited, skip it
cards/7/items/3: Process the node: add it to the result if the floor matches
cards/7/items/4: Push all children of the node onto the stack
cards/7/explain: The stack replaces function calls, and the visited set breaks rings. The traversal order comes out mirrored for children; if it matters, push children in reverse order.
cards/8/q: Fill in the walk: "push onto the stack", "pop from the stack" and "remember the visited node".
cards/8/explain: HashSet.Add returns false if the item was already there. One call both checks and remembers. With Contains, the node would never get into the set.
cards/9/q: Which level check is the most sensible for heights in meters?
cards/9/explain: Pick the tolerance by meaning: 1 cm for a building. Equals on a float is the same exact comparison as ==. Casting to int drops the fraction: 2.9999 becomes 2 while 3.0 becomes 3. And <= lets everything below the level through.
cards/9/wrong/1: It is the same exact comparison as ==. The only difference is NaN: NaN.Equals(NaN) is true, while NaN == NaN is false.
cards/9/wrong/2: Dropping fractions produces errors of a whole meter.
cards/9/wrong/3: That checks "not above", not "on the level".
cards/10/q: Match each symptom with its fix.
cards/10/pairs/0/1: RemoveAll or a copy of the list
cards/10/pairs/1/0: The process suddenly exits during a tree walk
cards/10/pairs/1/1: Stack and HashSet instead of recursion
cards/10/pairs/2/0: A floor looks empty, though it has elements
cards/10/pairs/3/0: Removal is slow on thousands of items
cards/10/pairs/3/1: One pass instead of Remove in a loop
cards/11/title: For seniors: what else was forgotten
cards/11/body: After RemoveResolved (and after Import) the queries in _cache stay old: the clash is already gone from the list, but the cache still returns it. Any change to _clashes must reset the cache, or the cache must store a data version number.
cards/11/deep: An iterative walk moves the "stack of plates" from the thread stack (around a megabyte) to the heap, where there is far more room. "Visited" marks can also live on the nodes themselves (say, a pass number): no HashSet and no allocations, but two concurrent walks will then get in each other's way. If the tree is edited from another thread, walk an immutable snapshot.
